posts.title: The Super Eagles' World Cup history: highs, lows and unforgettable moments
posts.excerpt: From USA 1994 to Russia 2018, Nigeria's World Cup journeys have given fans joy and heartbreak. Here's the story so far.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Nigeria first qualified for the FIFA World Cup in 1994 and has played in several tournaments since, reaching the round of 16 three times (1994, 1998 and 2014). The team has thrilled fans with its flair, but has also had painful exits and missed qualifications.

USA 1994: a dazzling debut

In their first World Cup, Nigeria topped a group that included Argentina and Bulgaria. In the round of 16 they led Italy until the final minutes, before Roberto Baggio's late goals sent Italy through. The world fell in love with the Super Eagles' attacking style.

France 1998: Spain stunned

Nigeria beat Spain 3–2 in one of the most memorable games of the tournament, with Sunday Oliseh's long-range strike becoming iconic. They topped their group again but lost to Denmark in the round of 16.

2002 and 2010: early exits

In Korea and Japan in 2002, and South Africa in 2010, Nigeria went out in the group stage, despite talented squads.

Brazil 2014: back to the knockouts

Under Stephen Keshi, fresh from winning AFCON 2013, Nigeria reached the round of 16 again, before losing to France.

Russia 2018: close but not enough

Nigeria beat Iceland but lost a tense final group game to Argentina, going out in the group stage.

Missing out

Nigeria missed the 2006 and 2022 World Cups, which hurt fans deeply. Each qualifying campaign is now watched closely by Nigerians at home and abroad.

The diaspora's World Cup

For Nigerians abroad, World Cup games are huge social events. Fans gather in homes, restaurants and community halls, often in full green-and-white, and many have travelled to tournaments to support the team.

The bottom line

Nigeria's World Cup story is full of brilliance and heartbreak. The dream of going further than the round of 16 lives on.

posts.title: Freelancing and remote work from abroad: what Nigerians need to know
posts.excerpt: Want to keep working for Nigerian clients or start a side hustle after moving? Your visa may not allow it. Here's what to check first.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Many people want to keep freelancing for Nigerian clients or start a side hustle after moving abroad. But your visa conditions decide what work you can do. Some visas restrict self-employment or extra work. Breaking the conditions can put your immigration status at risk, so check carefully before you start.

Why your visa matters

Every visa comes with conditions. In the UK, for example:

  • Skilled Worker and Health and Care Worker visas generally allow work for your sponsor, with limited additional work allowed in certain circumstances. Self-employment is usually not permitted.
  • Student visas usually limit working hours during term time and don't allow self-employment or freelancing.
  • Graduate visas usually allow most work, including self-employment.
  • Dependant visas often allow work, but check your specific conditions.
  • Indefinite Leave to Remain and citizenship generally remove these restrictions.

Rules differ in Canada, the US and other countries too.

Working for Nigerian clients while living in the UK

Some people assume that working remotely for a foreign client doesn't count. Immigration rules can still apply to work you do while physically in the UK, and tax rules apply too. Get advice before you take on remote work alongside a sponsored job or student visa.

Tax

If you're UK resident and earn self-employment income, you usually need to register with HMRC and file a Self Assessment tax return. Income earned abroad can also be taxable in the UK depending on your residence status.

Safer ways to build a side income

  • Wait until your visa allows self-employment
  • Focus on skills, certifications and networking in the meantime
  • Check if your visa allows permitted additional work in your sponsored field

The bottom line

Before you take on any side work, read your visa conditions and get advice if unsure. Protecting your status matters more than any extra income.

posts.title: Nigeria's Independence Day: how the diaspora celebrates 1 October
posts.excerpt: Every 1 October, Nigerians abroad wear green and white, cook jollof and celebrate. Here's the history and how diaspora communities mark the day.
posts.content:
Quick gist: Nigeria gained independence from British rule on 1 October 1960. Every year, Nigerians at home and abroad celebrate with parades, parties, church services, cultural shows and plenty of jollof. In diaspora cities, it's a day to show pride and pass culture on to children.

A short history

On 1 October 1960, Nigeria became an independent nation, with Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa as prime minister. In 1963, Nigeria became a republic. The years since have brought civil war, military rule and the return to democracy in 1999, but Independence Day remains a symbol of national pride.

How the diaspora celebrates

  • Community events: associations host dinners, galas and cultural nights
  • Church and mosque services: prayers for Nigeria
  • Parades and festivals: some cities host Nigerian festivals and parades around the date
  • Schools: some children do presentations about Nigeria
  • Social media: a sea of green-and-white profile pictures and throwback photos

Ideas for families

  • Cook a traditional meal together
  • Watch a Nollywood classic or a documentary about Nigeria's history
  • Teach children the national anthem and pledge
  • Video call relatives back home
  • Wear traditional outfits to school or work events

Mixed feelings

For many people, the day is also a time to reflect on challenges at home. Celebrating while hoping for change is part of the diaspora experience.

The bottom line

Whatever you feel about the state of things, 1 October is a day to celebrate being Nigerian and to share that pride with the next generation.
